explanation.text: When two fractions have the same bottom number, their parts are the same size. The fraction that takes more of them is the greater.
When two fractions have the same top number, they take as many parts each. A whole cut into fewer parts has bigger parts, so the fraction with the smaller bottom number is the greater.
Say the comparison in words first. Then write the sign with its open side towards the greater fraction, or the sign of two equal fractions when they are the same.
Not every number shares out exactly. When it does not, some is left over, and that is the remainder.
To divide, find the greatest product of the times table of the number you divide by that is not more than the number shared. How many times it goes is the quotient, and what is left is the remainder.
The remainder is always smaller than the number you divide by. If it is not, one more group still fits.
Check by multiplying back. The quotient times the number you divide by, and then the remainder added, give the number you began with.
In a story, ask what the remainder is. Sometimes it is what is left over, and sometimes it still needs a place of its own.
A fraction names equal parts of a whole. The bottom number says how many equal parts the whole is cut into, and the top number says how many of them you take.
To find a fraction of a number, share the number into as many equal parts as the bottom says. That is one part. Then take as many parts as the top says.

The same part of a whole can be written as more than one fraction. A fraction is in lowest terms when no number but one divides both its top and its bottom. To get there, divide them both by the same number.
A times table counts up in equal steps. To multiply is to count equal groups, so many groups of the same size, and the product is how many there are in all of them.
The order does not matter. Three groups of five are as many as five groups of three, so each fact of the table is two facts at once.
A division undoes a multiplication. To share a number into equal groups, find the fact of the table whose product it is, and the missing number of that fact is the answer.
When a fact is slow to come, count up in steps from a fact you know, out loud, and stop at the one the line asks for.

count-up.description: Say the times table of the number out loud until you reach the product you need.
count-up.title: Count up in steps

draw-the-parts.description: Draw the whole cut into equal parts, and shade the parts that the fraction takes.
draw-the-parts.title: Draw the parts

undo-it.description: To check a division, multiply back: the groups times the size of a group, plus what is left, is where you began.
undo-it.title: Undo it

greater-bottom-greater-fraction.description: Took the fraction with the greater bottom number for the greater one, as if the bottom numbers were whole numbers to compare.
greater-bottom-greater-fraction.trap_advice: A whole cut into more equal parts has smaller parts. Picture the two wholes cut up before you compare.

not-in-lowest-terms.description: Wrote a fraction of the right value that can still be reduced.
not-in-lowest-terms.trap_advice: Look for a number that divides both the top and the bottom, and divide them both by it.

one-part-only.description: Found one equal part of the number where the fraction takes several of them.
one-part-only.trap_advice: Find one equal part first, then take as many of them as the top of the fraction says.

remainder-left-out.description: Left out what was left over where the story still needs a place for it.
remainder-left-out.trap_advice: Ask what happens to what is left over. If it still needs a place of its own, count that place too.

remainder-not-added.description: Built the number shared again from the groups alone, without adding what was left over.
remainder-not-added.trap_advice: The number shared is the groups times their size, and then what was left over added to it.

remainder-too-big.description: Left a remainder as large as the number divided by, or larger.
remainder-too-big.trap_advice: Check that the remainder is smaller than the number you share by; if it is not, one more fits.

reversed-comparison.description: Wrote the sign for the other way round: greater for less, or less for greater.
reversed-comparison.trap_advice: Say the comparison in words first, then write the sign whose open side faces the greater number.

times-table-slip.description: Took the product of a neighbouring fact of the times table, one step too far or too short.
times-table-slip.trap_advice: Count up in the number you multiply by, out loud, until you reach the fact you need.

took-away.description: Took one number from the other where the line multiplies or divides.
took-away.trap_advice: Taking away does not find a factor or a share. Ask how many groups of the same size make the number.

top-and-bottom-swapped.description: Wrote the number of all the equal parts on top and the parts taken below.
top-and-bottom-swapped.trap_advice: The bottom number says how many equal parts the whole has, and the top says how many of them you take.

wrong-operation.description: Added where the line multiplies or divides, or multiplied where it adds.
wrong-operation.trap_advice: Say the line in words, as groups of the same size, then count what the groups make.
